title: I was embarrassed when I got caught “goofing off.”
author: Ruth Poulsen
summary: Ruth Poulsen, a school principal recovering from burnout, begins with the embarrassment she felt when a teacher found her sitting quietly in her office, although she was actually thinking through how to support a student and his family. From that moment she draws two countercultural mindsets for high-achieving schools. First, rest is an integral part of excellence, since constant action is efficient but not effective, and chronic stress erodes the empathy teachers need for relational work. Second, treating people like machines harms both adults and students, which she supports with the Mayo Clinic's list of stress-related health harms and a recess study in which 15 more minutes of recess left children with one third the hair cortisol. She borrows a model from her father's regenerative farm, where land rests four years in every nine, and argues schools need similar rhythms. She closes with practical steps for leaders, such as modelling reflection, interrogating the master schedule and setting a school-wide digital sunset.
points: Constant action may be efficient, but efficiency is not effectiveness, and a pause before answering an angry email can prevent more problems than it solves.
Chronic stress erodes empathy, the very skill teachers need most, so teacher rest is a condition for relational learning and not a perk.
Students are not machines either: a study found that 15 extra minutes of recess left children with about one third the accumulated hair cortisol.
The regenerative farm model of letting land rest four years in nine offers a picture of healthy rhythms of work and rest for schools.
Leaders carry the first responsibility by modelling reflection, pruning the master schedule and setting a digital sunset.
quotes: Constant action might be efficient, but the deeper truth is this: efficiency is not effectiveness.

Giving myself down time to breathe, to regulate my emotional response, to reflect on the problem and on the complex interwoven relationships surrounding the problem: that down time was the opposite of goofing off.
But the truth is, strategies without relationships are barren. Real learning is profoundly relational.
When a teacher is operating under the chronic stress of constant action, their empathy is eroded, the very skill they need most for the complexity of teaching.
The students with a mere 15 minutes more of recess per day had on average accumulated one third the amount of cortisol in their hair as students with less recess.
This is the regenerative paradigm: not worshiping only at the altar of productivity, but intentionally valuing health and mutual flourishing.
The voices saying we need to choose between educator thriving and student achievement are simply inaccurate. A thriving leader has more capacity to foster a thriving school culture.
It takes courage to model a regenerative pace that might be counter-cultural at your school. It’s not easy to go against the grain.
